analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to share vehicle data and repair tools with owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan right-to-repair bill with 56 cosponsors split evenly between the parties cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in November 2023, but the full committee never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The REPAIR Act would bar car manufacturers from blocking owners, their chosen mechanics, or aftermarket parts makers from accessing the data, software, and repair information needed to fix modern vehicles. It would require manufacturers to share repair data and tools at fair and reasonable cost, stop them from forcing the use of their brand of parts outside warranty and recall work, let owners pick their own towing and repair shop, and give the Federal Trade Commission power to enforce these rules. Today, as cars have turned into computers on wheels, manufacturers can lock repair data behind proprietary systems, steering repairs to dealerships and their own networks.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners and lessees, who could get their cars fixed at independent shops or do the work themselves without paying for manufacturer-locked data access or being told they must use brand-name parts. Independent repair shops, tow companies, and aftermarket parts makers also gain, because they get guaranteed access to the diagnostic data and technical information needed to work on newer vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must give owners and their designees access to vehicle-generated data without restrictions, fees, licenses, or being forced to use a manufacturer's decryption device [S3].
Manufacturers must make critical repair information and tools available to owners, independent repair facilities, and aftermarket parts makers at a fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory cost [S3].

Outside of recall and warranty repairs, manufacturers cannot mandate or imply a mandate to use their brand of parts, tools, or equipment, and any brand recommendation must carry a notice that owners can choose what to buy [S3].
Owners cannot be blocked from using the towing or repair provider of their choice, and contracts that try to waive these rights are void [S3].

If a car uses wireless telematics, manufacturers must make repair data directly and wirelessly available through a standardized access platform, administered by an independent entity not controlled by manufacturers [S3].
Violations are enforceable by the Federal Trade Commission, with a complaint process and a five-month deadline for orders [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers bear the cost of opening their data and repair information systems, and lose some of the repair revenue that comes from steering owners to dealerships. Dealer service departments and manufacturer-authorized repair networks lose business when owners can choose independent shops. Aftermarket data and tool providers pay to build and secure the shared access platform.

drawbacks.text: Cybersecurity risk: opening up real-time vehicle data to more parties creates more entry points for attackers, though the bill explicitly allows manufacturers to keep cryptographic protections and directs NHTSA to write security standards [S3].

The bill preempts state laws that impose narrower duties on manufacturers and overrides any state law requiring use of a particular brand of parts or tools, which could roll back state-level repair rules some consumers currently rely on [S3].

Implementation is slow: key rules take up to two years to write, and the most valuable telematics data access only begins a year after the final rule, so owners of cars bought in the meantime get limited immediate benefit [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most drivers the benefits are concrete: lower repair bills, freedom to pick a mechanic or tow service, and no forced purchases of brand-name parts outside warranty work. The real costs fall on automakers and their dealer networks, not on the public. The main design risks are cybersecurity and a two-year wait for full rules, and the preemption clause is a genuine tradeoff since it overrides some state repair laws. On balance a reasonably designed bill whose main cost is borne by the industry that currently holds the data.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House subcommittee by voice vote in November 2023, but the full Energy and Commerce Committee never took it up and it died when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 9, 2023 by Rep. Neal Dunn (R-FL) with bipartisan original cosponsors, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1].
It drew 56 cosponsors, split evenly at 28 Democrats and 28 Republicans [S4].
On November 2, 2023, the Innovation, Data, and Commerce Subcommittee held a markup and forwarded the bill to the full committee by voice vote [S5].
The full Energy and Commerce Committee never held a markup or vote on the bill, and no floor action ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers keep exclusive control of the vehicle data and repair information that decides where cars can be fixed, and dealership service departments keep the repair business that independent shops never gained access to. Drivers keep paying the resulting higher repair costs.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers and their dealer service networks

sides.party_line_note: Support was evenly split, with 28 Republican and 28 Democratic cosponsors, and the subcommittee advanced it on a voice vote; the opposition that mattered was not partisan but the committee leadership's decision never to schedule a full vote.

industries.note: The bill strips manufacturers of exclusive control over vehicle-generated data and critical repair information, requiring them to hand it over at fair cost and ending their ability to steer repairs to their own networks. Their loss is the driver's gain: cheaper, freer repair choices.

industries.industry: Independent auto repair shops and tow companies
industries.note: Shops get guaranteed access to diagnostic data, software, and repair tools needed for modern vehicles, letting them compete with dealerships on newer cars. Owners get more options and lower prices.

The bill bars manufacturers from blocking compatible aftermarket parts and from mandating brand-name parts outside warranty work, expanding the aftermarket's market and keeping repair prices down for owners.

Dealer service centers lose the captive repair revenue that comes from owners having no alternative when independent shops cannot access the data. Consumers' savings come largely out of their margins.
